measurement.happened:
This week in Ukraine was dominated by a brutal cycle of Russian strikes on energy infrastructure and civilian targets, Ukraine's escalating campaign against Russian oil refineries, and the final diplomatic preparations for US-brokered peace talks in Abu Dhabi. Let me walk through the major threads.

**Russian strikes on energy and civilian targets (the dominant story).** Russia launched what multiple sources described as massive overnight missile and drone barrages on Kyiv and surrounding regions, hitting power substations, a major bridge, and logistics infrastructure. Hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians lost electricity, and Kyiv was plunged into darkness. Zelensky and the Kyiv mayor publicly traded blame over the city's blackout, which added a layer of domestic political friction. In the south, a Russian strike on an aid center in Zaporizhzhia killed at least 53 people (the toll kept climbing from 26 to 31 to 40 to 53 across multiple reports), making it one of the deadliest single attacks of the war. A hospital, a hospice, and a school used as an aid shelter were also hit. Russia also targeted emergency crews responding to the strike, which Kyiv called a double-tap attack, and shared bodycam footage. Zelensky warned that Russia's strikes are designed to cut Ukraine in half. The cumulative effect is that steel production shut down, grain exports stalled, and the economy is being choked. (Supported by: Reuters Nov 6-9, AP Nov 2-9, BBC Nov 1-9, CNN Nov 3-8, DW Nov 1-9, TV5Monde Nov 1-9, Bloomberg Nov 3-9, FT Nov 9, Al Jazeera Nov 3-9, CNBC Nov 1.)

**Ukraine's counter-strikes on Russian refineries and logistics.** Ukraine hit at least six Russian oil refineries in the span of the week, including Saratov, Ryazan, and Yanos, plus a hub of the e-retailer Ozon in southern Russia. Zelensky confirmed the campaign is continuing. The result is visible: Russia is rationing petrol in several regions, shipping metal via the Arctic to evade Ukrainian strikes, and its diesel is reportedly going unsold. This is Ukraine's most effective economic lever this year, and it is clearly designed to squeeze Russia just before the talks. (Supported by: Reuters Nov 4-9, Bloomberg Nov 3-9, FT Nov 9, Al Jazeera Nov 5-6, CNBC Nov 1.)

**Abu Dhabi talks and the Trump-Melania diplomatic push.** The US announced it will mediate trilateral talks between the US, Ukraine, and Russia in Abu Dhabi the following week. Russian diplomats and military officials confirmed they will attend. European foreign ministers, including France's Kallas, said they will join. Trump met Putin's top envoy at the White House and called the prospective deal 'big and beautiful.' Melania Trump hosted both Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House, positioning herself as an 'exclusive intermediary' on a local ceasefire and calling for a 'more enduring' truce. Zelensky awarded Melania a state honour and expressed gratitude. The talks are expected to focus on security guarantees for both sides. (Supported by: Reuters Nov 2-9, AP Nov 2-9, BBC Nov 5-9, CNN Nov 3-7, DW Nov 5-9, TV5Monde Nov 5, Bloomberg Nov 2-9, FT Nov 7-8, Al Jazeera Nov 3-9, CNBC Nov 3.)

**US midterms and the 'Blue Wave.'** The November 3 US midterm elections produced a Democratic sweep in Congress. Ukraine bonds jumped on the news. Zelensky said Ukraine must adapt to new US political realities and hopes the Democratic Congress will bring more aid and scrutiny of Russia. Analysts framed it as a potential shift in US foreign policy on Ukraine, Iran, and Israel. The Kremlin, meanwhile, expressed hope that the election shake-up would not shift Trump's negotiating posture. (Supported by: Reuters Nov 4-6, CNN Nov 4-6, DW Nov 4, TV5Monde Nov 4, Bloomberg Nov 4, FT Nov 7, Al Jazeera Nov 5, CNBC Nov 4.)

**Cyber warfare and information attacks.** Both Ukraine and Russia reported that their emergency alert apps were hacked, with fake nuclear attack warnings issued to civilians on both sides. Hacked records revealed an estimated 400,000 Russian military deaths. Pro-Russian hackers targeted Italy's foreign minister. A Belarusian source claimed to have obtained data on Russian losses. The information war is clearly intensifying alongside the kinetic one. (Supported by: Reuters Nov 6, AP Nov 2, BBC Nov 2, DW Nov 2-3, TV5Monde Nov 1, Bloomberg Nov 2, CNBC Nov 2.)

**Kherson ceasefire ends, fighting resumes.** The longest localized ceasefire of the war, in the Olechky/Kherson sector, ended around November 1-2. Civilians prepared for the return of heavier Russian attacks. The ceasefire had been brokered with Melania Trump's involvement, and its end is a blow to the diplomatic narrative. (Supported by: Reuters Nov 1, BBC Nov 1-2, DW Nov 2, TV5Monde Nov 2, Al Jazeera Nov 1.)

**European diplomacy and funding fights.** The G7 foreign ministers met in Paris, pressing US Secretary Rubio on Ukraine and Iran. Germany's Merz threatened to block the EU budget over Ukraine funding and issued an ultimatum. Meloni warned Europe risks irrelevance in the peace talks and criticized the EU's 'disjointed' approach. Italy shipped fresh military aid despite a coalition split. Germany proposed an extra 100 million euros for Ukrainian infrastructure. A first multinational military exercise for a potential postwar Ukraine force was held in Poland. Ukraine's EU membership path is lagging behind Moldova's. (Supported by: Reuters Nov 5-9, AP Nov 9, BBC Nov 3, DW Nov 3-9, TV5Monde Nov 5, Bloomberg Nov 5-9, FT Nov 5, 7, 9, Al Jazeera Nov 6.)

**IMF and financial support.** The IMF launched a loan review that could unlock 1.67 billion dollars for Ukraine. Donors at a Paris meeting promised half the funding for repairing the Chernobyl arch. The US pushed to restore Russian gas sales to Europe via Ukraine, a move that will be politically sensitive in Kyiv. (Supported by: Reuters Nov 9, TV5Monde Nov 9, WSJ Nov 2.)

**Domestic political friction and corruption.** Zelensky publicly criticized the SBU security service over a corruption scandal. Senior security and police officials were accused of running a criminal ring. A military recruitment dorm saw clashes. Zelensky and the Kyiv mayor traded blame over the blackout. These are signs of internal strain under wartime pressure. (Supported by: Reuters Nov 5-7, BBC Nov 3.)

**Military and strategic developments.** Russia is reportedly using its own version of Starlink for military communications over Ukraine. Ukraine is adapting to Russian jet-powered drones. Russian land gains are dwindling while its army suffers record losses, with 350 conscripts killed in a single period. Palantir is harvesting battlefield data that Ukraine pays for 'with blood.' Finland is considering Ukraine-style tank barriers. (Supported by: Reuters Nov 6, DW Nov 7, TV5Monde Nov 6, Bloomberg Nov 2, Al Jazeera Nov 5-6, FT Nov 7.)
measurement.expected:
Looking at the week of November 9 through roughly November 16, here is what I expect, theme by theme, with my confidence level.

**Abu Dhabi trilateral talks (almost certain).** The US, Ukraine, and Russia will sit down in Abu Dhabi, with European diplomats joining. This was announced multiple times this week, delegations are confirmed, and both sides have been striking hard in the days before, which is classic pre-talks posturing. The agenda will center on security guarantees, the scope of any ceasefire, and whether a broader 'all of Europe' deal is on the table. I expect the talks to produce a joint communique or a framework document, but not a signed peace agreement. Zelensky has already flagged that the security deal floated by Trump could be 'potentially dangerous,' so there will be friction. Russia will likely insist on no concession on territory. I rate the talks happening as almost certain, producing a tangible document as probable, and producing a full ceasefire deal as possible but not probable.

**Continued Russian strikes on energy (almost certain).** Russia has been hitting power infrastructure daily this week and Zelensky warned of more strikes on energy targets, bridges, and infrastructure. With winter heating season approaching and the talks happening, Russia has both the motive (pressure) and the means (missiles, drones) to keep striking. I expect at least one major overnight barrage on Kyiv or surrounding regions during the week, leaving hundreds of thousands without power. Confidence: almost certain.

**Ukraine's refinery campaign continues (probable).** Ukraine has hit six refineries in a week and Zelensky confirmed the campaign is ongoing. Russia is already rationing fuel. I expect at least one or two more Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries or logistics hubs, particularly in the Volga region or southern Russia. This is Ukraine's most effective economic weapon and it would be odd to pause it during talks. Confidence: probable.

**Post-talks diplomatic scramble (almost certain).** Whatever comes out of Abu Dhabi will trigger a cascade of statements from Trump, Zelensky, Putin, Meloni, Merz, Kallas, and others. I expect a mixed reception: Western allies pushing for a stronger European role, Russia testing the waters, and Ukraine trying to lock in security guarantees. The G7 meeting in Paris this week will set the European tone. Confidence: almost certain that there is a flurry of diplomatic statements and follow-up meetings.

**IMF review progresses (probable).** The IMF launched its review on November 9. These processes typically take a few weeks, but I expect staff-level consultations to begin or be ongoing during this period. The 1.67 billion dollar unlock is not immediate but the process is now in motion. Confidence: probable that the review is actively underway; almost certain that it is not yet concluded.

**Winter heating crisis becomes more acute (probable).** With hundreds of thousands already without power, heating season is here, and Russian strikes are targeting the grid, I expect growing public complaints, possible localized rationing of electricity in some regions, and Zelensky or regional governors making public appeals for generators and emergency aid. The Madrid summit appeal for energy infrastructure aid will gain urgency. Confidence: probable.

**Cyber incidents continue (possible).** The alert app hacks and the 400,000-casualty data leak show both sides are active in cyberspace. I expect at least one more notable cyber incident, possibly targeting energy SCADA systems, government websites, or another round of fake alerts. Confidence: possible.

**European military preparation (probable).** The first multinational exercise in Poland has started. I expect additional training exercises, logistics planning, and political discussions about the composition and mandate of a potential postwar European force in Ukraine. This is a long-term project but the groundwork is being laid now. Confidence: probable that planning and exercises continue; unlikely that a full deployment decision is made this week.

**Domestic political friction (possible).** The SBU corruption scandal, the recruitment dorm clashes, and the Zelensky-mayor blame game suggest internal tensions are rising. I expect at least one more public spat or a minor reshuffle in the security apparatus, but not a full-blown crisis. Confidence: possible.

**US congressional dynamics (probable).** The new Democratic Congress will likely hold early hearings or issue statements on Ukraine aid, possibly pushing for Patriot systems or a more structured aid package. Zelensky's comment about solving the 'Patriot air defence issue' suggests this is a live negotiation. Confidence: probable that the new Congress makes noise about Ukraine in its first days.

**Less likely surprises I would watch for:**
- A sudden Russian proposal to extend the Kherson ceasefire as a goodwill gesture before or after Abu Dhabi (possible but not probable).
- A major Ukrainian drone or missile strike on a Russian capital or a high-profile target like Moscow or St. Petersburg as a pre-talks signal (possible).
- A second cyberattack on critical Ukrainian infrastructure, such as a bank or a hospital network (possible).
- Zelensky making a surprise visit to Washington or Brussels to meet the new Congress or EU leaders in person (possible).
- A minor escalation in the Black Sea, such as a naval engagement or a mine incident, given Russia hit three ships this week (possible).

**Things I would not bet on:**
- A full ceasefire or peace agreement being signed in Abu Dhabi (unlikely; both sides are still far apart, and the 'no concession' framing from Al Jazeera suggests hard positions).
- A major ground offensive by either side in a new sector (unlikely; both are focused on the talks and the energy war).
- Zelensky resigning or a major cabinet reshuffle (unlikely; the corruption scandal is serious but not yet at that level).
- A nuclear incident or a shift in the nuclear dimension of the war (unlikely; no signs of that in the headlines).
- A full EU membership decision for Ukraine (unlikely; the process is slow and the FT notes Ukraine is behind Moldova).
- A major natural disaster or a new pandemic hitting Ukraine specifically (unlikely).
emoji_reasons: The defining feature of this week was the relentless Russian bombing of Ukrainian energy infrastructure, bridges, hospitals, and an aid center that killed over 50 civilians, making airstrikes and explosions the central experience for Ukrainians.

The entire diplomatic architecture of the week was built around the upcoming Abu Dhabi peace talks, Melania Trump's hosting of both delegations, and Trump's 'big beautiful deal' rhetoric, making peace negotiations the dominant political storyline.

Hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians lost electricity, Kyiv went dark, the grid was hit repeatedly, and the winter heating crisis is intensifying, making the power grid and blackouts the most tangible daily reality for ordinary people.

delta.motion: The most dramatic growth between the two photographs is in the violence of the war itself. In the first week, Russian strikes were described as brutal and frequent, with a train station hit in Dnipro killing about 15 people. By the second week, Russia had launched what multiple sources called massive overnight barrages on Kyiv, plunging the capital into darkness and leaving hundreds of thousands without power. A single strike on an aid center in Zaporizhzhia killed at least 53 people, the deadliest single attack of the war, and Russia hit emergency crews responding to the blast in what Kyiv called a double-tap. The energy infrastructure thread went from a concern to a crisis: steel production shut down, grain exports stalled, and Zelensky warned Russia is trying to cut Ukraine in half. Ukraine's refinery campaign grew from a politically fraught pause-and-resume cycle into a sustained, visible economic squeeze. In the first week, the strikes were a friction point with Washington. In the second week, Ukraine hit at least six refineries in a single span, Russia is rationing petrol in several regions, shipping metal via the Arctic to dodge Ukrainian drones, and its diesel is reportedly going unsold. The diplomatic thread grew from a hope into a concrete plan: where the first week had Trump saying a trilateral meeting would be set up soon, the second week has Abu Dhabi talks confirmed for the following week, with Russian diplomats and military officials attending, European foreign ministers joining, Melania Trump hosting both delegations at the White House, and Trump calling the prospective deal big and beautiful. European funding and diplomacy grew from pledges into action: the G7 foreign ministers met in Paris, Germany threatened to block the EU budget over Ukraine funding, Italy shipped fresh military aid, and a first multinational military exercise for a potential postwar Ukrainian force was held in Poland. The IMF launched a loan review that could unlock 1.67 billion dollars. A whole new thread appeared in the second photograph that was barely visible in the first: cyber warfare. Both Ukraine and Russia reported their emergency alert apps were hacked, with fake nuclear attack warnings sent to civilians on both sides. Hacked records revealed an estimated 400,000 Russian military deaths. Pro-Russian hackers targeted Italy's foreign minister. This information war was a minor footnote in the first week and a major story in the second. Another new thread is the US midterm elections, which produced a Democratic sweep in Congress on November 3. Ukraine bonds jumped, Zelensky said Ukraine must adapt to new US political realities, and analysts began debating whether the shift would change aid levels and the tone of negotiations. This was completely absent from the first photograph. Domestic political friction in Ukraine grew as well. The first week had smaller items like a retail chain losing its entire store network and the economy projected to shrink. The second week has Zelensky publicly criticizing the SBU security service over a corruption scandal involving senior officers, a military recruitment dorm seeing clashes, and Zelensky and the Kyiv mayor openly trading blame over the capital's blackout. What shrank is the Oleshky story. In the first photograph it was the single dominant story: 2,000 people evacuated, emotional reunions after up to 1,711 days of separation, global coverage, a rare humanitarian pause. By the second photograph, the ceasefire had ended around November 1-2, fighting resumed, and the story had shifted from hope to the grinding reality of the front returning. The Starlink-Musk dispute, a significant side-story in the first week, faded almost entirely, replaced by the quieter but more strategic development of Russia deploying its own version of Starlink for military communications over Ukraine. The Patriot missile delivery, a major item in the first week, did not reappear as a headline in the second, suggesting it was quietly executed. The Nord Stream trial, the Ugandan and Malagasy soldiers, the EU-Canada alliance, and the Finland-Norway phone calls with Putin all vanished from the second photograph as distinct threads. The Black Sea, which had Turkey warning both sides and Al Jazeera reporting dead dolphins, did not produce a prominent incident in the second week. The overall motion is from a week dominated by a single humanitarian event and a web of diplomatic signals to a week defined by escalating kinetic violence, a concrete diplomatic deadline, a new cyber front, and the ripple effects of a US election that no one in the first photograph could have foreseen.
delta.wind: The expectations were broadly well-calibrated on the military and diplomatic tracks, but they missed several important developments and over-weighted a few. On the almost-certain items: the Oleshky evacuation did continue to generate news, but in a different form than expected. The forecast assumed the evacuees would be processed, housed, and integrated, generating positive humanitarian coverage. Instead, the ceasefire ended around November 1-2, and the news shifted to fighting resuming and civilians bracing for heavier Russian attacks. The humanitarian story became the story of its end. The local ceasefire held for about a week, which matches the expectation that it would hold for a few more days, but it collapsed rather than expanding. Patriot deliveries were expected to be announced or confirmed, and they likely happened quietly, but the second photograph does not feature them as a headline, so this came true in a muted, almost invisible form. Russian drone and missile attacks continued at high frequency and actually escalated, with the Zaporizhzhia aid center strike and the Kyiv blackout being more severe than the forecast anticipated. Ukraine's refinery strikes continued, and the pause-and-resume cycle with Washington seems to have resolved in Ukraine's favor, with six refineries hit in a week without the expected US pushback. The cycle that was predicted to repeat at least once did not repeat in the same form. The Starlink dispute did fade, as expected, but it evolved into a more strategic question about Russia using its own satellite network. The EU funding and alliance threads did see follow-up, but the EU-Canada alliance faded as a distinct story while the broader EU funding fight (Germany blocking the budget, G7 pressure) became the main thread. On the probable items: the Trump-Zelenskyy-Putin trilateral meeting was announced and scheduled for Abu Dhabi, which is exactly what was expected, and it came through with even more detail than the forecast anticipated, including Melania's role and European participation. The European defense spending pledges did generate parliamentary debates and concrete actions, including Germany's budget ultimatum and the first multinational postwar force exercise. Ukraine's offensive claims were partially corroborated by the observation that Russian land gains are dwindling and its army is suffering record losses. The Black Sea incident was expected but did not prominently materialize in the second photograph. On the possible items: the Oleshky ceasefire did not expand to a broader pause; it ended. The new wave of Russian ballistic missile strikes did come, and was more severe than expected. Ukraine's economic shrinkage did trigger policy responses, including the IMF loan review and the Chernobyl arch funding round. The Nord Stream trial did not produce a visible procedural development in the second week. On the unlikely-but-worth-watching items: a major cyberattack did materialize, with both sides' alert apps hacked and fake nuclear warnings issued, which was a genuine surprise in terms of scale and simultaneity. The US pushing to restore Russian gas sales via Ukraine is a form of conditioning aid on concessions, which was flagged as unlikely but did appear. The less-likely surprises mostly did not materialize: there was no dramatic new Starlink restriction, no single high-level European leader making a dramatic direct appeal, no new African or Asian country announcing troop deployment, and no special legal status for Oleshky evacuees. The things the forecast said it would not bet on largely held: no general ceasefire, no major Ukrainian breakout, no Starlink trade dispute, no Russian pullback, no nuclear or chemical incident, no EU membership treaty, no decisive US congressional vote (though the midterms were a related but different event), and no major new offensive in Donbas or Zaporizhzhia. The biggest blind spot in the expectations was the US midterm elections. The first photograph was taken on November 1, and the elections were on November 3, just two days into the forecast window. The expectations did not mention them at all, yet the Democratic sweep in Congress became a major factor affecting Ukraine bonds, aid expectations, and the tone of the Abu Dhabi talks. This suggests that for Ukraine, US domestic political events are a recurring source of surprise that the forecast framework should weight more heavily. The second blind spot was cyber warfare, which was not mentioned in the expectations at all but became a significant thread in the second week. The third was the depth of domestic political friction in Ukraine, with the Zelensky-SBU corruption dispute and the Zelensky-mayor blame game being more prominent than the expectations anticipated. Overall, the forecast was solid on the known threads but under-weighted the intersection of US domestic politics, cyber operations, and Ukrainian internal governance, all of which can shift the picture within a single week.
delta.driver: The force pushing Ukraine from the first photograph to the second is the collision of two clocks: the military clock of winter and the diplomatic clock of Abu Dhabi. Russia is trying to break Ukraine's energy infrastructure before the cold deepens, because a population without power in December is a population that is harder to defend and harder to keep fighting. Ukraine is trying to squeeze Russia's economy through its refinery campaign, because a Russia that is rationing petrol and shipping metal over the Arctic is a Russia that enters the talks with a tighter budget and a more urgent need for a deal. Both sides are, in effect, raising their stakes in the two weeks before the trilateral meeting, knowing that whatever they achieve on the ground will set the floor for what they will accept at the table. The US midterm elections added a third clock: a Democratic Congress that is more likely to scrutinize Russia and press for aid, which changes the political arithmetic in Washington and gives both Kyiv and Moscow a new reason to move quickly or to stall. Melania Trump's self-appointed role as intermediary, Zelensky awarding her a state honor, and the White House hosting both delegations are not just diplomatic theater; they are the US trying to own the process before a new Congress can reshape it. The underlying driver, then, is a race: both sides are trying to maximize their position in the kinetic domain while the diplomatic domain is being assembled, and the winter season is the deadline that makes the race urgent. Everything else, the cyber attacks, the corruption scandal, the Black Sea, the EU budget fight, is downstream of that central competition between the front and the table.

I expect Zelensky to publicly acknowledge the US proposal while privately pushing back, and for the new Democratic Congress to use the issue to assert its oversight role. The refinery campaign is not just a military operation; it is a negotiating position, and its tempo will be calibrated to the diplomatic calendar.

CYBER WARFARE AND THE INFORMATION FRONT (medium-high confidence of at least one more incident; medium confidence of it becoming a headline): Both sides' emergency alert apps were hacked this week, with fake nuclear attack warnings sent to civilians. Hacked records revealed an estimated 400,000 Russian military deaths. Pro-Russian hackers targeted Italy's foreign minister. This is a new and growing front that the previous forecast underweighted. I expect at least one more cyber incident this week, possibly timed around the Abu Dhabi talks to create pressure, confusion, or a pretext for a side to claim the other is not in good faith. The 400,000 deaths figure will be the subject of a media war: Russia will contest the number, Ukraine and its allies will try to verify it through independent sources, and the figure will be used in the talks as a marker of Russian losses. The hacked alert apps will generate public frustration on both sides and may lead to a temporary switch to SMS or radio alerts. I expect at least one European official to make a public statement about the cyber attacks, linking them to the broader information war. The cyber front is not a side story; it is a parallel battlefield that will shape the tone of the talks and the public perception of each side's credibility.

US DOMESTIC POLITICS AND THE NEW CONGRESS (medium confidence of visible congressional activity; low confidence of a major policy shift): The Democratic sweep in the November 3 midterms is a new variable that the previous forecast completely missed. The new Congress is in its first weeks and will be asserting its oversight role. I expect at least one Ukraine-related headline from Washington this week: a hearing, a statement from the new Senate or House leadership, or a question about the Abu Dhabi process. The Democratic Congress is more likely to scrutinize Russia and press for aid, which changes the political arithmetic in Washington. Ukraine bonds jumped on the midterm results, and I expect them to continue benefiting from the new political climate. However, Trump is still President, and the new Congress will not be able to unilaterally reshape policy in its first week. The effect is more about tone and pressure than about concrete legislative action. I expect the new Congress to use the Abu Dhabi talks as a test case for its oversight role, with at least one Democratic senator or representative making a public statement about the process. The US push to restore Russian gas sales via Ukraine will be a point of congressional friction, with Democrats potentially questioning why the US is re-opening a pipeline to Russia while also squeezing Russia's oil sector. The midterm effect is real but gradual; it will shape the next several months more than this single week.

DOMESTIC POLITICAL FRICTION IN UKRAINE (medium confidence of continued headlines): Zelensky publicly criticized the SBU security service over a corruption scandal involving senior officers, traded blame with the Kyiv mayor over the capital's blackout, and a military recruitment dorm saw clashes. The wind tells me I have been underweighting this. I expect the corruption scandal to generate at least one more headline this week, possibly involving a new arrest, a parliamentary question, or a public statement from a senior official. The blame game over the blackout will continue as restoration efforts are slow and the cold deepens. Zelensky faces the challenge of projecting unity and confidence for the Abu Dhabi talks while managing internal dissent. The recruitment dorm clashes are a small but telling sign of strain in the military's social fabric. I expect Zelensky to make at least one public statement addressing domestic concerns, possibly framing the corruption fight as a sign of strength rather than weakness. The domestic friction is not a crisis, but it is a recurring source of headlines that will complicate the narrative of a unified Ukrainian delegation at the talks.

EUROPEAN DIPLOMACY AND FUNDING (medium confidence of at least one headline; low confidence of a major decision): Germany's budget ultimatum over Ukraine funding, the G7 pressure on US Secretary Rubio, the IMF loan review that could unlock $1.67 billion, and the first multinational military exercise for a potential postwar Ukrainian force are all active threads. The wind tells me European stories tend to fade faster than I expect. I expect at least one European funding or diplomatic headline this week, but I should not bet on a major EU decision. The IMF review is a slow process; the $1.67 billion will not be unlocked this week, but the review itself will generate a headline. The Chernobyl arch funding round, with donors promising half the cost, is a smaller, more concrete item that may generate a follow-up. The multinational military exercise in Poland will produce a report or a statement, but it is a background item. Germany's budget ultimatum is the most likely to generate a headline, as Merz has threatened to block the EU budget over Ukraine funding. I expect at least one European foreign minister to make a public statement linking the Abu Dhabi talks to European security guarantees. The EU membership path for Ukraine remains slow, and I do not expect a major step this week.

MILITARY AND STRATEGIC DEVELOPMENTS (medium confidence of at least one headline): Russia is reportedly using its own version of Starlink for military communications over Ukraine. Ukraine is adapting to Russian jet-powered drones. Russian land gains are dwindling while its army suffers record losses, with 350 conscripts killed in a single period. Palantir is harvesting battlefield data. Finland is considering Ukraine-style tank barriers. These are quieter but strategically significant developments. I expect at least one of these to generate a headline this week. Russia's satellite network is a structural development that will become more visible as the war drags on. The jet-powered drones are a new threat that Ukraine is still adapting to, and I expect at least one incident involving them. The Russian losses figure will be contested and used in the information war. Palantir's data harvesting is a behind-the-scenes development that may generate a corporate or defense-industry headline. Finland's tank barriers are a smaller, more concrete item that may generate a European defense headline.

WHAT I WOULD NOT BET ON: A full peace deal or comprehensive ceasefire signed in Abu Dhabi. A major Ukrainian ground offensive capturing a Russian-held city. A dramatic US congressional vote on Ukraine aid levels in the first week of the new Congress. Russia pulling back from any front or making a major territorial concession. A nuclear or chemical incident. Zelensky resigning or being removed from power. A full EU membership treaty for Ukraine. A major Black Sea naval incident involving a sinking or a collision. A new African or Asian country announcing troop deployment to Ukraine. A full resolution of the SBU corruption scandal. A complete restoration of Kyiv's power grid within the week. A second-city ceasefire brokered by Melania Trump that holds for more than a few days. A formal US government inquiry into the Starlink issue. A new wave of Ukrainian strikes on Russian targets within 100 km of Moscow (though a strike within 200 km is possible).
crystal.headline: Abu Dhabi Talks Loom as Ukraine's Grid Burns and Russia's Refineries Bleed
emoji_reasons: The US-brokered trilateral peace talks in Abu Dhabi are the defining event of the week, with both sides entering from positions of maximum pressure and a new Democratic Congress watching.

Russia's escalating strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure, including the 53 killed in Zaporizhzhia and Kyiv's blackout, continue to dominate the military narrative and set the stakes for the talks.

Ukraine's sustained campaign against Russian oil refineries, with six hit in a week and Russia rationing petrol, is the most effective economic lever in the war and will shape the diplomatic calculus.
crystal.tldr: The Abu Dhabi trilateral talks between the US, Ukraine, and Russia are the central event of the week, with both sides entering from positions of maximum pressure after a week of record Russian strikes and Ukraine's most aggressive refinery campaign yet. Expect a framework or process agreement rather than a full deal, continued Russian strikes on energy infrastructure, at least one cyber incident, and the new Democratic Congress beginning to assert its oversight role. The talks will be read through the lens of winter's approaching deadline and the new US political reality.
crystal.eli5:
Next week, the big thing is a meeting in Abu Dhabi where the US, Ukraine, and Russia sit down together to try to talk about peace. Both sides are trying to look strong before the meeting: Russia has been bombing Ukraine's power plants really hard, and Ukraine has been bombing Russia's oil factories. Think of it like two kids about to share a toy, and each one is trying to show the other they can break it first.

The meeting will probably not end with a perfect peace deal. More likely, they will agree to keep talking, maybe pause fighting in one small area, and write down some ideas. That is actually normal for this kind of meeting. The new US Congress, which now has more Democrats, will be watching closely and probably asking questions about whether the deal is fair for Ukraine.

Meanwhile, the war keeps going. Russia will probably keep bombing power plants because it is getting cold and they want Ukraine to be more desperate. Ukraine will probably keep hitting Russian oil factories because it is their best way to make Russia feel the pain. There will also be more hacking and fake alerts on phones, which is a new kind of fighting that is getting worse.

The main thing to watch is whether the meeting produces something real, even if it is small, or whether it just produces a lot of photos and a statement that says 'we will keep talking.' Either way, it is the most important thing happening in Ukraine next week.

judgment.reading_a: Forecast A got the broad strokes of the week right in several important ways. Its 'almost certain' section correctly identified the high frequency of Russian drone and missile attacks (which dominated the week), Ukraine's deep-strike drone campaign against Russian refineries (six refineries hit, including Saratov, Ryazan, and Yanos), the Kherson ceasefire as fragile and potentially collapsing (it ended around November 1-2), and the Oleshky story continuing to generate news (though in the form of the ceasefire ending rather than ongoing processing). The 'probable' section nailed the Abu Dhabi trilateral talks being announced or scheduled, the Black Sea seeing at least one incident (Russia hit three ships), and European defense spending generating parliamentary debates (Merz's ultimatum, Germany's extra 100 million euros). The 'possible' section correctly flagged a new wave of Russian ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv (the massive overnight barrages) and the economy shrinking triggering a policy response (IMF loan review of 1.67 billion dollars). The 'unlikely but worth watching' section hit on the major cyberattack on critical infrastructure (both sides' emergency alert apps hacked with fake nuclear warnings) and the Black Sea ships. The Zimbabweans arrested trying to join the war echo the 'new African country sending troops' surprise. The Patriot issue was named specifically and Zelensky did mention solving it. However, A's 'almost certain' section included the EU SAFE fund seeing follow-up and Patriot deliveries being announced, neither of which clearly materialized this week. The 'possible' section's Oleshky ceasefire expanding to a broader Kherson front pause went the wrong direction (it ended, not expanded). The Nord Stream trial procedural development and the dispute over the suspect's command were not visible in the week's headlines. The 'things not to bet on' list was largely correct: no general ceasefire, no major Ukrainian ground breakout, no Starlink trade dispute, no EU-Ukraine membership treaty. A few misses: the acute Starlink dispute did not fully fade (Starshield contract expiring was noted, Russia using its own version of Starlink), and the 'pause-and-resume cycle with Washington' was only partially visible. Overall, A captured the kinetic and diplomatic skeleton of the week well but was somewhat generic in its European diplomacy and financial mechanics, and a couple of 'almost certain' items did not clearly land.
judgment.reading_b: Forecast B's thematic structure tracked the week's actual narrative more closely. Theme 1 (Abu Dhabi Summit) was almost exactly right: the talks were announced for the following week, Russia confirmed attendance, Europeans (Kallas) said they would join, Trump met Putin's envoy and called the deal 'big and beautiful,' and Melania positioned herself as an intermediary. The 'Zelensky making further concessions' and 'security guarantees' framing matched the actual talks focus. Theme 2 (Winter Energy Crisis) was the strongest hit: the prediction of a major blackout in Kyiv lasting 24 to 72 hours, emergency measures, and the cumulative economic choke (steel shutting down, grain exports stalling) all materialized precisely. The Zaporizhzhia aid center strike killing 53 people, the double-tap on emergency crews, and the hospital and hospice hits all fit the 'Russia willing to hit civilian hubs' framing. Theme 3 (European Financial Mechanics) was partially right: the G7 meeting in Paris, Merz's ultimatum to block the EU budget, Meloni's warning about European irrelevance, Germany's extra 100 million euros, and the first multinational military exercise in Poland all fit. The 'European leaders asserting a visible role' was very accurate. However, the SAFE fund first activation and EU-Canada alliance producing a specific deliverable were not clearly visible. Theme 4 (Refinery Strike Cycle) was very accurate: six refineries hit, Russia rationing petrol, shipping metal via the Arctic, diesel going unsold. The 'less likely surprise' of a new strike capability or coordinated operation had some echo in the jet-powered drones and Palantir data harvesting. Theme 5 (Oleshky Aftermath) was partially right: the Oleshky template was cited in diplomatic conversations, but the ceasefire ended rather than being extended, and the prisoner exchange surprise did not materialize. Theme 6 (Starlink) was partially right: the Starshield contract expiring and Russia using its own version of Starlink kept the structural debate alive, but the specific congressional hearing and Musk statement did not appear. Theme 7 (Domestic and Peripheral) was a strong hit: the SBU corruption scandal with senior security and police officials accused of a criminal ring, the Zelensky-Kyiv mayor blame-trading over the blackout, and the military recruitment dorm clashes all fit. The 'less likely surprise' of a domestic political incident related to corruption was exactly right. The 'what not to bet on' list was largely correct. B's misses: the UN war-crimes inquiry follow-on, the EU-Canada alliance specific deliverable, the prisoner exchange, the Musk/Spacex statement, the retail chain destruction in consumer data, and the aerial rescue drones story were not clearly visible. B did not specifically flag the cyber warfare on emergency apps, the Black Sea ships, or the Zimbabweans, which A caught. The US midterms (Blue Wave) was a major story that neither forecast specifically predicted, though B's framing of 'US political realities' and the Kremlin's hope that the election wouldn't shift Trump's posture were captured in the actual reporting.
judgment.comparison: Both forecasts captured the week's dominant threads: Russian strikes on energy infrastructure, Ukraine's refinery campaign, the Abu Dhabi talks announcement, the Oleshky/Kherson ceasefire story, and European diplomatic maneuvering. The US midterms (Blue Wave) was a major surprise to both, though it was only two days after the forecast date. Forecast A had several specific hits that B missed: the cyber warfare on emergency alert apps (flagged as 'unlikely but worth watching'), the Black Sea ships being hit, the Zimbabweans trying to join the war, and the Patriot issue being named. These were real and notable stories. However, A's 'almost certain' section included items that did not clearly materialize (EU SAFE fund activation, Patriot delivery timelines), and its 'possible' section's Oleshky expansion went the wrong direction. Forecast B's strength was in specificity and narrative coherence. Its prediction of a major multi-day blackout in Kyiv, the cumulative economic choke, the European leaders asserting a visible role (G7, Merz ultimatum, Meloni warnings), the domestic political friction (SBU corruption, Zelensky-mayor blame), and the Russian economic squeeze (petrol rationing, Arctic shipping) all landed with high precision. B's 'less likely surprises' were generally more on-target: the domestic corruption incident, the European weapons/production deal, and the energy-sector ceasefire as a pre-summit gesture all had echoes in the actual week. B's thematic structure better captured how the stories interlocked: the energy crisis feeding into the talks, the European diplomacy as a reaction to being shut out, the refinery strikes as economic leverage before the talks. A was more list-like and hierarchical, which made its 'almost certain' section feel overconfident when some items did not land. B was more probabilistic in its language ('high,' 'medium,' 'low-medium') and this calibration was more accurate. The key differentiator is that B's high-confidence items were more consistently right, while A had a few 'almost certain' items that did not clearly materialize. B also better captured the domestic political dimension (corruption, blame-trading) and the European diplomatic specifics (G7, Merz, Meloni) that defined the week's non-kinetic narrative. A's specific catches (cyber warfare, Black Sea, Zimbabweans) were real but somewhat peripheral compared to the dominant stories. Both were solid forecasts, but B would have served a reader slightly better as a picture of the coming week because its high-confidence items were more reliably accurate and its thematic framing matched the actual narrative flow more closely. VERDICT: B
